Let \(s=\log x\). We solve for \(g\).

The proposed closed form is
\[
g(s)=\left(1+\frac{s^2}{24}\right)^{-2}.
\]
Check:
\[
g'(s)=-\frac{s}{6}\left(1+\frac{s^2}{24}\right)^{-3},
\]
and
\[
g''(s)=-\frac16\left(1+\frac{s^2}{24}\right)^{-3}
+\frac{s^2}{24}\left(1+\frac{s^2}{24}\right)^{-4}.
\]
Thus
\[
g''(s)+\frac5s g'(s)
=
-\left(1+\frac{s^2}{24}\right)^{-4},
\]
so
\[
g''(s)+\frac5s g'(s)+g(s)^2=0.
\]
Also \(g(s)\to1\) as \(s\to0^+\).

It remains to justify uniqueness. Multiplying the ODE by \(s^5\) gives
\[
(s^5g'(s))'=-s^5g(s)^2.
\]
Since \(g(s)\to1\), \(g\) is bounded near \(0\). Hence \(s^5g'(s)\) has a finite limit as \(s\to0^+\). If that limit were nonzero, then \(g'(s)\sim Cs^{-5}\), forcing \(g(s)\) to blow up like \(s^{-4}\), contradicting \(g(s)\to1\). Therefore
\[
s^5g'(s)=-\int_0^s t^5g(t)^2\,dt.
\]
Integrating once more,
\[
g(s)=1-\frac14\int_0^s\left(t-\frac{t^5}{s^4}\right)g(t)^2\,dt.
\]
This Volterra equation has at most one bounded solution near \(0\): for two solutions \(u,v\), if \(|u+v|\le B\) on \([0,r]\), then
\[
\sup_{0<s\le r}|u(s)-v(s)|
\le \frac{Br^2}{12}\sup_{0<s\le r}|u(s)-v(s)|.
\]
For small enough \(r\), this forces \(u=v\). Ordinary ODE uniqueness then extends equality to all \(s>0\).

Thus
\[
g(s)=\left(1+\frac{s^2}{24}\right)^{-2}.
\]
Since \(s=\log x\),

\[
\boxed{f(x)=\frac{1}{\left(1+\frac{(\log x)^2}{24}\right)^2}}.
\]
